answer_text:
There is a small inconsistency in the wording: a four-cycle in \(S_4\) has order \(4\), so an element \((\sigma,i)\) with \(\sigma\) a four-cycle and \(i\in \mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\) nontrivial has order

\[
\operatorname{lcm}(4,5)=20,
\]

not \(15\). An element of order \(15\) would instead come from a 3-cycle together with a generator of \(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\). In any case, \(G=S_4\times \mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\) contains elements of order \(20\), and that gives the decisive lower bound.

Let \(\sigma=(1\,2\,3\,4)\in S_4\) and let \(i\) be a generator of \(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\). Then

\[
(\sigma,i)\in S_4\times \mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z
\]

has order \(20\). If \(G\) embeds into \(S_n\), then \(S_n\) must contain an element of order \(20\).

In a permutation in \(S_n\), the order is the least common multiple of its disjoint cycle lengths. To get order \(20=4\cdot 5\), a permutation must have cycle lengths whose lcm contains both a factor of \(4\) and a factor of \(5\). The smallest possible disjoint cycle structure is therefore a 4-cycle and a 5-cycle, requiring at least

\[
4+5=9
\]

points. Hence no \(S_n\) with \(n\le 8\) can contain \(G\).

Now we construct an embedding into \(S_9\). Let \(S_4\) act naturally on \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) and fix \(\{5,6,7,8,9\}\). Let \(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\) act as the 5-cycle

\[
(5\,6\,7\,8\,9)
\]

on \(\{5,6,7,8,9\}\) and fix \(\{1,2,3,4\}\). Since these two actions are on disjoint supports, they commute and have trivial intersection. Thus we get an injective homomorphism

\[
S_4\times \mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z \hookrightarrow S_9.
\]

Therefore the smallest symmetric group containing \(G\) is

\[
\boxed{S_9}
\]
